messages.author: 30b406a9189eeb25
messages.subject: silly sweave
parts:
Hi,

After years of using sweave, I'm just now starting to realize how dumb it is to create a format (Rnw) that can be read neither by neither latex nor R. 

Yihui has brilliantly solved this by letting one write in vanilla latex, markdown, or html, while just sticking the code in the comments.  Would it be possible to do the reverse and write code in .R format that can be read by R, but have the markup as R-style comments using the syntax of latex, html, mardown, etc, such that an intepreter (knitr?) could read the R code and generate the desired html/pdf/etc?  (It seems this direction is closer to the original Doxygen/literate programming idea, though with Sweave-esque goal of creating dynamic documents, not just generating software documentation).  Do others think this would be useful?  Yihui, is this a possible extension of the knitr framework?

-Carl

--
Carl Boettiger
UC Davis
http://www.carlboettiger.info/

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] silly sweave
parts:
This is somehow related to a previous feature request:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/129 In that one, we want to
write R code and all "meta information" in LaTeX comments. I said that
was my ideal model, which I have not started to pursue yet.

I think it is possible to write everything in pure R; the function
stitch() as well as read_chunk() is a simple start and still far away
from this goal.

One thing that makes this "ideal model" seem inconvenient for pure R
is how to write normal texts. For example, you probably have to use a
sequence of # to comment out a text block like this

# start_r eval=TRUE
rnorm(10) + 1
# end_r

# I want
# to say
# something
# other than R

This looks cumbersome if there is a large amount of texts to write. In
that case, I'd rather use LaTeX or HTML directly. For small-scale
scripts, stitch() may be a good start. You can also externalize R
scripts as much as possible
(http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/externalization/), so you can run code
freely in separate files.

BTW, it was not Sweave that invented <<>>= and @ (bottom of
http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/minimal/), and it is undeniable that
Sweave has played an important role in history, so let's not say silly
:) In other places, though, this kind of home-made syntax seems to be
adopted by R, which I really dislike very much; two typical examples
are \dontrun{} and \donttest{} -- they can appear in Rd examples but
are not valid R code.

Regards,
Yihui
--

messages.author: 30b406a9189eeb25
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] silly sweave
parts:
Hi Yihui, list,

Good points, the lack of block commenting in R does make that more annoying, though with a decent text editor it shouldn't be too much of an issue.  I think it would be useful if something like your mock-up below was possible. 

Didn't mean to blame sweave, but cweb/noweb's introduction of a third language and formating seemed nicely avoided by subsequent literate programming like doxygen, while it's maintained in the sweave model ;)  Does anyone actually still use noweb?


On a more practical level, is it possible to have markdown R blocks appear as markdown codeblocks (or github-flavor-markdown code-blocks?)  instead of as html comments?  It's seems it might be nice to display the code on the source copy?

Carl

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] silly sweave
parts:
I do not know if anybody still uses cweb or noweb; I knew Sweave way
before I knew these ancient inventions. I was in kindergarten when
noweb was created... It was unfortunate that Sweave was a well-behaved
student of WEB, which has created a lot of inertia so it is difficult
to abandon the original syntax.

As for markdown codeblocks, the difficulty is to be able to identify
which block is *R* code since you cannot guarantee all are R code;
that is why we need a special marker. Besides, there has to be a way
to specify chunk options. That said, I believe it is possible to
customize the regexp patterns (http://yihui.name/knitr/patterns) so
that GFM and Jekyll code blocks can be identified because both have
beginning and ending patterns (like ```r and ```). For traditional
markdown (indent 4 spaces), it is not impossible either; you may end
up with

begin_r: label, opt1=value1, opt2=value2
rnorm(100)
end_r

and tell knitr your patterns are '^[ ]{4}begin_r:(.*)' and '^[ ]{4}end_r'.

If you need a concrete example, just let me know.

Regards,
Yihui
